lesson.text: Quick memory: last unit, the rock cycle. How does sedimentary rock form? Sediments settle in layers, then are squeezed and cemented.
Earth is about 4.6 billion years old. Scientists read its history in rock layers.
In undisturbed layers, the oldest are at the bottom and the youngest at the top: the law of superposition. Each layer was laid down on top of the one before.
Fossils in the layers show what lived when. Index fossils, of species that lived for a short time, help match layers in different places.

The geological time scale divides history into eras: dinosaurs lived in the Mesozoic; humans appeared only very recently. If Earth's history were one day, humans would arrive in the last few seconds before midnight.
Try it in the world: dig straight down beside a cliff in your world and note each layer you pass. In real rock, the deepest layer would be the oldest. Next: Earth's resources.

exercises.prompt: About how old is Earth?
exercises.hint: It is much older than a million years: think in billions.
exercises.explain: About 4.6 billion years.

exercises.prompt: In undisturbed rock layers, where are the oldest?
exercises.hint: Which layer was laid down first?
exercises.explain: At the bottom: it was laid down first.

exercises.prompt: Fossils can tell us what lived long ago.
exercises.hint: Remains in rock.
exercises.explain: Yes: fossils show past life.

exercises.prompt: Which era did the dinosaurs live in?
exercises.hint: Dinosaurs lived in the middle era of the three the lesson names.
exercises.explain: The Mesozoic era: the age of the dinosaurs.

exercises.prompt: Humans have been around for most of Earth's history.
exercises.hint: On the one-day clock, when do humans arrive?
exercises.explain: No: humans appeared only very recently.

exercises.prompt: A layer with trilobite fossils lies under a layer with dinosaur fossils. Which lived first?
exercises.hint: Lower is older.
exercises.explain: The lower layer is older: trilobites first.

exercises.prompt: What is an index fossil?
exercises.hint: It helps date layers.
choices: a fossil of a species that lived a short time
exercises.explain: A species that lived only a short time.

exercises.prompt: Why do scientists use index fossils?
exercises.hint: Same fossil, same age.
choices: to match layers in different places
exercises.explain: They match layers of the same age.

exercises.prompt: The law of superposition says younger layers lie on top of older ones.
exercises.hint: Layers pile up.
exercises.explain: Yes: each new layer settles on top of the older ones.

exercises.prompt: Lava cuts through three layers. Is the lava older or younger than them?
exercises.hint: The layers had to be there first.
exercises.explain: It cut through them, so it came later.

exercises.prompt: If Earth's history were one day, when would humans appear?
exercises.hint: Humans are about 300,000 years old; Earth is 4.6 billion. Is that a big or tiny part?
exercises.explain: In the last few seconds before midnight.

exercises.prompt: Layers are found tilted and folded. What does this show?
exercises.hint: Layers form flat.
choices: They were moved after they formed.
exercises.explain: Forces moved them after they formed.

exercises.prompt: The same index fossil is found in rock in Wales and in Canada. What does it tell you?
exercises.hint: Index fossils date layers.
choices: The layers are about the same age.
The rocks are the same colour.
exercises.explain: The layers formed at about the same time.

exercises.prompt: Rock layers can be missing where erosion wore them away.
exercises.hint: Wind, rain and rivers can wear rock away. What happens to a layer that is worn away?
exercises.explain: Yes: erosion can remove layers.

exercises.prompt: Order these, oldest first.
exercises.hint: Simple life came first.
exercises.explain: Single cells, fish, dinosaurs, humans.

exercises.prompt: The layers from the picture: order them from oldest to youngest.
exercises.hint: Remember the law of superposition: which layer was laid down first?
exercises.explain: The bottom layer is oldest, then the middle, then the top, the youngest.

exercises.prompt: Match each idea to what it tells scientists.
matches: far layers are the same age
exercises.hint: Think about what each clue shows about time or about what happened later.
exercises.explain: Superposition: lower layers are older. An index fossil: layers far apart are the same age. Tilted layers: moved after they formed. A missing layer: erosion wore it away.

exercises.prompt: Sort them: did they first appear before the dinosaurs, or after?
exercises.hint: Dinosaurs lived in the Mesozoic. Was each one much earlier, or much later?
exercises.explain: Before the dinosaurs: the first single-celled life, trilobites and the first fish. After them: woolly mammoths and, very recently, the first humans.

exercises.prompt: In a cliff, shale lies on sandstone. A crack of cooled lava cuts the sandstone but stops at the shale. Order the events.
exercises.hint: Lower layers are older, and anything that cuts a layer is younger than it. Did the lava cut the shale?
exercises.explain: The sandstone formed first (it is lower). The lava cut through it, so the lava came later. The shale is not cut, so it formed on top after the lava: sandstone, lava, then shale.

exercises.prompt: Mud settles 1 cm deeper every 100 years and hardens into a layer of rock. How many years did a layer 3 m thick take to form?
exercises.hint: Change 3 m into centimetres first, then use 1 cm for every 100 years.
exercises.explain: 3 m = 300 cm. At 1 cm every 100 years, that took 300 × 100 = 30,000 years. A thick layer can record a long stretch of time.
